title: The fire and the text
short: The Bradstreets' house at Andover, Massachusetts, burned on 10 July 1666; the poem survives in the family manuscript and was first printed in 1867.
body: The fire destroyed the family home, papers and a library of some 800 books. The poem was not in the 1678 Several Poems; it survives in the Andover manuscript, a family copy made by her son Simon, where it is headed as copied 'out of a loose paper'. John Harvard Ellis first printed the manuscript poems in his 1867 edition. The poem is written in iambic tetrameter couplets, a plain measure suited to private meditation. It moves from narrative (the fire), to lament (the ruins), to self-rebuke and consolation (the heavenly house): the pattern of Puritan spiritual meditation on a providence.

title: Let no man know
short: The cry of 'Fire!' is something she wishes no one ever to experience: 'Let no man know' is a prayer.
body: 'Let no man know, is my desire' means 'I wish that no one may ever hear that sound'. The inverted syntax of these lines ('I wakened was', 'the light did spy') is characteristic of the poem, and partly a result of the demands of rhyme and metre; some readers find it awkward, others hear in it the formality of a verse testimony.

sources.cite: John Harvard Ellis, ed., The Works of Anne Bradstreet in Prose and Verse (Charlestown, 1867)

title: succorless
short: Without help: she prays that God will not leave her 'succourless' (the archive prints it as two words).
body: 'Succor' (succour) means help or relief in need; 'succourless' is helpless, without aid. The prayer for strength in distress uses the language of the Psalms, where God is a 'very present help in trouble' (Psalm 46:1). Her first response to the fire is thus not to save goods but to cry to God, as a godly Puritan was expected to do.

title: gave and took
short: From Job 1:21: 'the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD.'
body: Job's words on hearing of the loss of his property and children were the classic text for Christian resignation under affliction. Bradstreet 'blest his name', exactly as Job does. Lines 15-18 continue the argument: the goods were God's own, not hers, and he was just in taking them ('so 't was just'). 'Repine' (l. 18) means to complain or fret discontentedly.

sources.cite: "Verses upon the Burning of Our House", Wikipedia

title: Stewardship
short: Her goods were only lent by God; he had a right to take them all, yet left 'sufficient' for the family.
body: The Puritan doctrine of stewardship held that all property belongs to God and is lent to its holders. 'He might of all justly bereft' means 'He might justly have bereft us of everything', yet he left enough. This is the poem's first, formal resolution; the following section shows that the feeling has not yet caught up with the doctrine. The neat logic of these lines is that of a sermon applying doctrine to experience.

sources.cite: Jeannine Hensley, ed., The Works of Anne Bradstreet (Cambridge, Mass.: Harvard University Press, 1967)

title: The ruins
short: The second movement: walking past the ruins, she remembers where things stood, and grief returns.
body: After the dutiful resignation of the first section, the poem admits a renewed sense of loss as she sees the places where she sat and lay, where the trunk and chest stood, and the 'store I counted best'. The concrete objects ('that trunk ... that chest') make this the most vivid passage in the poem. 'My pleasant things' echoes Lamentations 1:10 and Isaiah 64:11 ('all our pleasant things are laid waste'), passages lamenting the destruction of Jerusalem and the Temple.

title: Apostrophe to the house
short: She addresses the burnt house directly ('thy roof', 'thee'), listing the domestic life that will never happen there again.
body: The shift to 'thy' turns the poem into an elegy for the house. The negative catalogue (no guest, no tale, no candle, no bridegroom's voice) recalls the prophetic curses on cities where the sounds of daily life will cease. The section ends 'In silence ever shalt thou lie', returning to the silence of the opening line. The address to an abandoned dwelling is a classical and biblical topos as much as a personal outburst.

title: bridegroom's voice
short: Echoes Jeremiah 7:34 and 16:9: God will cause 'the voice of the bridegroom' to cease in the desolated land.
body: Jeremiah repeatedly warns that God will silence 'the voice of mirth, and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom, and the voice of the bride'. In Bradstreet's household this may also have a literal sense: weddings of her children might have been celebrated in the house. The allusion links domestic loss to the prophetic theme of judgement, suggesting the fire is a chastening providence.

title: Adieu ... all's vanity
short: From Ecclesiastes 1:2: 'vanity of vanities; all is vanity': earthly things are empty and transient.
body: 'Vanity' in the biblical sense means emptiness, futility (Hebrew hebel, breath, vapour). The double 'Adieu' is a farewell to the house and to worldly attachment. The line closes the lament and prepares the turn of the next line. Ecclesiastes was traditionally ascribed to Solomon, the king who had possessed everything and found it empty, which makes it a fitting text for someone who has just lost a well-furnished house.

title: The turn: self-rebuke
short: The third movement: she rebukes her own heart in a series of questions, in the manner of a Puritan meditation.
body: 'Straight' means immediately; 'gan' is 'began'. Self-address ('my heart') and self-questioning were standard in Puritan devotional practice, modelled on the Psalms ('Why art thou cast down, O my soul?', Psalm 42:5). The speaker now treats her grief as a spiritual fault: had she fixed her hope on earthly wealth? The questions are rhetorical: the expected answer to each is no, and the answer leads to the consolation that follows.

sources.cite: Jeannine Hensley, ed., The Works of Anne Bradstreet (Cambridge, Mass.: Harvard University Press, 1967)

title: the arm of flesh
short: A biblical phrase for merely human strength, contrasted with trust in God (2 Chronicles 32:8; Jeremiah 17:5).
body: In 2 Chronicles 32:8 Hezekiah says of the Assyrian king, 'With him is an arm of flesh; but with us is the LORD our God'; Jeremiah 17:5 curses the man who 'maketh flesh his arm'. 'Mouldering dust' (l. 39) recalls Christ's warning against treasure that moth and rust corrupt. Together the phrases name the two false trusts: possessions and human power.

anchor: That dunghill mists away may fly
title: dunghill mists
short: Worldly cares are vapours rising from a dunghill: low, foul and transient, obscuring the view of heaven.
body: The image contrasts the earthly with the heavenly: thoughts raised 'above the sky' will see past the mists that rise from the dung of earthly things. The dunghill was a common figure of worthless worldly goods (compare Paul counting all things 'but dung', Philippians 3:8). The line therefore asks for a clearing of spiritual vision: once the mist lifts, the heavenly house of the next lines becomes visible.

sources.cite: Jeannine Hensley, ed., The Works of Anne Bradstreet (Cambridge, Mass.: Harvard University Press, 1967)

title: a house on high
short: The burnt house is replaced by an eternal one in heaven: 2 Corinthians 5:1, 'a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens'.
body: Paul contrasts 'our earthly house of this tabernacle' with 'a building of God, an house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens' (2 Corinthians 5:1), and Christ promises 'In my Father's house are many mansions' (John 14:2). 'That mighty Architect' echoes Hebrews 11:10, of the city 'whose builder and maker is God'. The heavenly house is 'richly furnished' and 'permanent', answering point for point the lost house and its furniture.

anchor: It's purchased, and paid for, too
title: purchased and paid for
short: The heavenly house has been bought by Christ, the price his death; it is hers 'by his gift', not by her merit.
body: The commercial language (purchased, paid, price) answers the earlier concern with goods and 'store'. 1 Corinthians 6:20 says 'ye are bought with a price'; Puritan theology stressed that salvation is purchased by Christ and given freely by grace. 'Him who hath enough to do' means 'Him who has means enough to pay'; 'A price so vast as is unknown' is the infinite cost of the atonement.

sources.cite: Jeannine Hensley, ed., The Works of Anne Bradstreet (Cambridge, Mass.: Harvard University Press, 1967)

title: pelf
short: Pelf: money or riches, usually with a contemptuous sense of 'filthy lucre'.
body: 'Pelf' (from Old French, booty, spoil) was used by moralists and satirists for wealth viewed with contempt. Her farewell to 'pelf' and 'store' completes the ironic reversal of 'There lay that store I counted best' (l. 26). The word helps mark the poem's final distance from the possessions she earlier lamented. The repeated 'farewell' answers the 'Adieu, adieu' of line 36: the first farewell was to the house in grief, the second to wealth itself in resolve.

sources.cite: John Harvard Ellis, ed., The Works of Anne Bradstreet in Prose and Verse (Charlestown, 1867)

anchor: My hope and treasure lie above
title: treasure ... above
short: Echoes Matthew 6:19-21: 'lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven ... where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.'
body: The final couplet resolves the poem with a direct echo of the Sermon on the Mount, and it inverts line 27 ('My pleasant things in ashes lie'): now it is hope and treasure that 'lie', but above. Critics differ on how complete this resolution is. Some read the poem as a successful exercise in Puritan submission; others see the vividness of the lament as evidence that attachment to the world is only overcome by effort, so that the ending is a willed act of faith rather than a feeling achieved.

title: Metre and syntax
short: Iambic tetrameter couplets with frequent inverted word order, the plain style of Puritan verse meditation.
body: The poem is in rhymed couplets of four stresses (aa bb). Many lines invert normal word order to place the rhyme word last ('For sorrow near I did not look', 'I wakened was with thundering noise'). Commentators note that the inversions can sound odd to modern ears; they also give the poem a deliberate, formal gravity. The plain style was a Puritan ideal: verse in the service of truth and devotion, not ornament.
